t: What Keeps the Fire? Here Are Two Skillsets that Motivated Career Educators Have in Common
q: Externally, teaching affords us the unmatched privilege of contributing to the education of human beings. Few endeavors are as wrought with possibility as the teaching of people.
Internally, teaching is so difficult — emotionally, socially, intellectually, spiritually, physically — that it affords us rich soil within which to cultivate the inner life.
What happened was difficulty that we hadn't bargained for. We knew it would be hard — but 2020 hard? Poor administrator hard? Initiative fatigue hard? Cameras off hard? Endless paperwork hard?

The difference is skilled and thoughtful inner work, in two particular areas: depressurization and workload modification. Folks who are good at these two things tend to love and be good at their jobs and their lives.
But if you're only good at depressurization, you're not necessarily going to be a good teacher. Being good at your job and a generally depressurized person takes another skill: workload modification.

If you do everything you're "supposed" to do, just as you're "supposed" to do it, they know you'll work eighty-plus hours per week and you won't last very long. These people aren't playing a short game, though. This is their life's work.

And as they learn, their abilities improve: they can focus better, streamline better, satisfice better, skip better. Things that used to cost them lost sleep become simply parts of the job, pieces of the puzzle they're still working out.

t: Computer Feedback That Helps Kids Learn About Math and About Themselves
q: The prime directive of feedback is, per Dylan Wiliam, to “cause more thinking.” Evaluative feedback fails that directive because it doesn’t attach sufficient meaning to a student’s thought to cause more thinking.

Certainly, this makes an attempt at attaching meaning to a student’s thinking that the other examples so far have not. But the meaning is often an expert’s meaning and attaches only loosely to the novice’s. The student may have to work as hard to understand the feedback (the word “coordinate” may be new, for example) as to use it.

We make no assumption that the student understands what the problem is asking, or that we understand why the student gave their answer. We just attach as much meaning as we can to the student’s thinking in a world that’s familiar to them.

This “interpretive” feedback is the kind we use most frequently in our Desmos curriculum, and it’s often easier to build than the evaluative feedback, which requires images, conditionality, and more programming.
We’re building worlds. I’m not overstating the matter. Educators build worlds in the same way that game developers and storytellers build worlds.
Every time you work to attach meaning to student thinking, you help students learn more math and you help them learn about themselves as mathematical thinkers.

You help them understand, implicitly, that their thoughts are valuable. And if students become habituated to that feeling, they might just come to understand that they are valuable themselves, as students, as thinkers, and as people.

t: Routines: before a lesson and after a task
q: Effective routines make great classroom teaching possible. I have previously written about general routines that can transform the classroom culture and atmosphere for the better, when executed consistently. In this post, I will share routines for students before they start the lesson and after they finish a task.

As I enter a classroom, students know to be ready by opening their booklets and exercise books. I remind them of the topic and page number we are on for that lesson and they then know to write the title of the section down and answer the review questions in silence and from memory.

When students complete their work, they raise their hand and place it back down again. This tells me very quickly if most students have finished a task. To distinguish this action with a raised hand for a question, I instruct students to hold a pen to signal task completion and to leave their hand empty when raising their hand to ask a question.

This is something that requires training to ensure students know exactly what you expect of them. I always model how I expect students to answer a type of question and I ask them to practice on mini-whiteboards before they work on similar questions independently. The beauty of mini-whiteboards is that I can quickly check if all students are following instructions correctly and if not, I can support them and re-model if necessary.

As students work through questions, inevitably some will finish earlier than others. In these cases, students either sit while waiting for their peers to finish (wasted learning time) or they answer more questions from the booklet that I may have planned for them to complete in a future lesson.

I tell my students to either ‘Think back’ or ‘Look Forward’. When they ‘think back’, students self-quiz using the core questions for the topic we are working on or redo questions they didn’t get right the first time in a previous lesson.
I am still developing these routines but there is no doubt they have made life easier. This means I can focus on teaching well and students know what to expect at each stage of the lesson.

At the start, students open their booklets and answer review questions silently from memory while she sets up the room, with paired quizzing or a read-then-quiz for low-confidence classes as fallbacks.
To tell when work is finished while she cannot circulate, students raise a hand holding a pen, kept distinct from a question hand.
She reminds students of the success criteria before independent practice and uses mini whiteboards to model and check that they follow instructions.

q: But removing the bare minimum standard is a mistake that does a disservice to the very students he’s trying to help.
Removing the possibility of failure sends the message to students that they’re incapable of overcoming difficulties. They’re not good enough or tough enough or resourceful enough to find a way.
Ensuring everyone a passing grade proves to them that you don’t believe in them. You don’t think they can do it and therefore must give them a free pass.
For the tough-minded students who would rather crawl through broken glass than get a handout, pulling students who put in no effort up to their level is a slap in the face.
Given the chance, many students in want of nothing, who have few obstacles to overcome to complete their work, will check out along with (just about) everyone else.
Equality doesn’t mean removing standards. That’s inequality, and it leads to horrible outcomes. Equality in education means giving every student the opportunity to do challenging work.

t: How To Prevent Covid From Creating A ‘Lost Generation Of Students’
q: Back in the spring, experts predicted that the switch to remote learning would have a serious negative impact, especially on students who are Black, Hispanic, diagnosed with disabilities, learning English, or who come from low-income families. We now know those dire predictions were largely on target, leading a former secretary of education to express concern about “a lost generation of students.

Another study drew on data from a digital math platform called Zearn, which was serving approximately 925,000 students in kindergarten through fifth grade before the pandemic. The study found a huge socioeconomic divergence that hadn’t existed previously: kids from wealthier families were doing more math than before, while those from poor families were doing less.
Well-intentioned as they are, proposals like that can do more harm than good. Kids do need time to play, and they can acquire scientific knowledge from nature.
The vast majority of schools teach reading comprehension as a set of skills: finding the main idea, making inferences, etc. Those skills are what reading tests purport to measure.

Kids from more highly educated families—who are generally also wealthier—are able to pick up academic knowledge and vocabulary at home, whether or not they acquire it at school. That gives them a better chance of understanding the passages on reading tests, which aren’t tied to the content of the school curriculum.

We now have readily available elementary literacy curricula that are organized by topic rather than “skill,” and that cover meaty subjects in history, science, and the arts as well as literature. They cost no more than the old “skills”-focused curricula that haven’t worked, and some of them are even available for free.
A more realistic approach is to use explicit writing instruction, beginning at the sentence level, to build knowledge and compensate for gaps.

t: "Cameras On… Please?" Ideas for Turning Empty Squares into Faces
q: This isn't going to be me wading into the Great Camera Debate of 2020 but is instead me processing strategies for getting more students to turn their cameras on during whole-class, synchronous instruction.
It's not about me stealing student autonomy or micromanaging student bodies or depriving children of privacy. But I do desire to teach and know my students, and seeing them helps me in that work.
As soon as you start using the language of compliance or consequences, you're trading behavior for motivation. Behaviors can be coerced, but motivation can't.

The most remarkable thing that I found in my survey is that the most common reason cited by my students for not wanting their cameras on is that they don't like how they look. That one made me quiet for a few days.

As students arrive, admit and greet them individually, and check in with them about camera use. You might be able to check in with only a few students before needing to 'admit all,' but those who arrive early and have their cameras on will gain comfort from being in a small group to start.
Normally, I say that we teachers need more techniques and strategies like we need lobotomies: not much. Instead, we need clearer thinking and a deeper understanding of the work that matters the most.

In this case, I've got a novel problem called the Great Ghost Plague of Zoomland, and so I'm looking for efficient means through which I can gain insight into the problem and run small experiments on solving it.

t: Sandcastles v. the Himalayas: On Weak and Strong Boundaries
q: The trouble is that a lot of this boundary talk ends up being just that: talk. We talk about them, we share them with a friend, we say we'll do them, we make sure students or parents know about them… and then we transgress them.
In other words, we make sandcastle boundaries. They're pretty — but wimpy, too. A bit of self-indulgence rain, a rogue crashing wave of workload, and whoosh — bye bye, boundaries.

What we need are Himalayan boundaries: the kinds of things that life can't move so easily, that require Herculean effort to overcome. South Asian history is in some ways the story of how a boundary like the Himalayas made possible the development of a unique set of human cultures.

Setting a rule for yourself that you'll check email only one time per day, and when you do, you'll OHIO — only handle it once. Deleting email apps off your smartphone and then asking your friend or spouse to password-protect app downloading on your phone.

I've told them that limiting my work to these times is a most serious matter to me — it's what's keeping me from realizing my potential as an educator, from getting the breakthroughs that I need for "more learning, less stress.

In all of this, what you and I want is to look back on well-shaped careers and well-shaped lives. But the default modern life isn't one that works like that: instead it's frantic, frenetic, self-indulgent, crazed.
So: sandcastles won't work for what we're after. It's time to find some mountains.

t: What International Tests Can Tell Us About How To Improve Education
q: After the first administration of the PISA in 2000, Finland’s top ranking turned it into a beacon of hope for other countries, including the U.S. So-called “edutourists” flocked to the country in hopes of discovering its secret education sauce.

But in 2006, Finland’s PISA scores began a steady and significant decline. And some have pointed out that there’s a time lag between the adoption of education policy and the performance of 15-year-olds on tests.

One little-noticed result of the 2018 PISA, at least in the U.S., was the emergence of Estonia as the new Finland. The country came out at or near the top on all three subjects—math, reading, and science—and has done relatively well in narrowing the test-score gaps between socioeconomic groups.

As Crato notes, it’s not that teacher-directed instruction is always best. But there’s quite a bit of evidence that it’s far more efficient when students have little preexisting knowledge about a topic.

In her chapter, Spanish education expert Montse Gomendio argues that the lack of national tests in that country has led to serious inequity: struggling students can’t be identified and given remediation, and the result is a huge number of students who are forced to repeat a grade because they can’t keep up with the work.

Perhaps the lesson of the American experience is that—as Crato says in his introduction—“everything starts with curriculum.” Tests won’t accomplish much without a content-rich, rigorous curriculum in place—and pedagogical approaches that are tailored to the knowledge and skills of students.

q: Workload and pressure work together deviously to demoralize and demotivate even the best teachers. Here's how it works.

The best way to solve this is to develop expertise because expertise is what gives you the clarity you need to focus, reduce, simplify, skip, and satisfice — all the moves expert educators make in order to turn the default workload setting into something that is productive and manageable.
So, you need clarity and time in order to produce the expertise that will enable you to have clarity and time… that's one paradox.
We've known for a long time that in all areas of life, humans are capable of withstanding only so much pressure. You need some pressure if you're to perform optimally — but too much wipes you out.

Since our default condition is hyper-pressurization, and since hyper-pressurization makes us worse at our jobs, we end up managing our default teacher workloads extra poorly, and so our workload contributes to the hyper-pressurization we already experience.
First of all, naming it helps. I call it the workload-pressure paradox. Having this language is important to me because I'm turning chaos into concepts.

Solving the workload-pressure paradox is less about our circumstances than it is about the people we're in the process of becoming. It's about meeting the defaults — of our work, of our lives — with clearer heads, lighter hearts, fuller selves, and settled wills.
x: A second, related paradox: because default life is hyper-pressurized, teachers end up managing their already-impossible workload poorly, which feeds pressure right back into the system.

Stuart names a self-reinforcing cycle: default teacher workload is structurally impossible, but escaping it requires expertise, and expertise requires the clarity and time that an impossible workload denies you.
